Genesis 1.audience: Israel first received Genesis as the opening of the books of Moses. They lived among peoples who worshipped the sun, moon, and stars—something Moses later warned them against (Deuteronomy 4:19). Genesis 1 does not name the sun and moon; it calls them "the greater light" and "the lesser light" (Genesis 1:16).

culture.title: The seven-day week
culture.text: Israel kept a seven-day week ending in the Sabbath rest, and the fourth commandment grounds that rest in the six days of creation (Exodus 20:8–11). The pattern of evening and morning in Genesis 1 matches the Israelite reckoning of a day from sunset to sunset (Leviticus 23:32).

Genesis 2.audience: For Israelite hearers, the rivers named in Eden included the Tigris (Hiddekel) and the Euphrates (Genesis 2:14), the two great rivers of Mesopotamia, east of the land of Israel.

culture.title: Naming as authority
culture.text: In the ancient world, giving a name expressed authority over what was named. Later in Scripture, kings renamed those placed under them—Pharaoh renamed Joseph (Genesis 41:45) and Nebuchadnezzar's officer renamed Daniel and his friends (Daniel 1:7).

culture.title: Irrigated gardens
culture.text: Gardens in the dry Near East depended on rivers and irrigation channels. A well-watered garden became a picture of plenty; the Jordan valley is later described as "even as the garden of the LORD" (Genesis 13:10).

Genesis 3.audience: Israel heard this account knowing the hard life it describes firsthand: farming stony ground with thorns and thistles, and the pain and danger of childbirth in a world without modern medicine.

culture.title: Clothing of skins
culture.text: Leather and animal skins were common materials for garments and coverings in the ancient Near East; the tabernacle itself was later covered with rams' skins dyed red (Exodus 26:14).

culture.title: Cherubim as guardians
culture.text: Winged guardian figures stood at the entrances of palaces and temples in the ancient Near East. In Israel, cherubim were woven into the tabernacle curtains and set above the ark of the covenant (Exodus 25:18–20; 26:1).

Genesis 4.audience: Israel's own economy combined the two ways of life described here—tending flocks and farming crops—and its law later required offerings from both (Leviticus 1–2).

culture.title: Firstlings and firstfruits
culture.text: Abel brought "the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof." Israel's law later claimed the firstborn of the flock and the fat of offerings for the LORD (Exodus 13:12; Leviticus 3:16).

culture.title: Blood vengeance
culture.text: In societies without a central police force, a family avenged the killing of its members. Israel's law later set up cities of refuge so that an accused killer could have a hearing before the avenger of blood (Numbers 35:9–12).

Genesis 5.audience: Genealogies mattered greatly to Israel, whose land, priesthood, and inheritance were all assigned by family line. This list traces the line from Adam to Noah.

culture.title: Ancient king lists
culture.text: Other ancient peoples kept lists of early rulers with enormous lifespans, such as the Sumerian King List. Genesis 5 is a family record rather than a royal list, and it repeats the refrain "and he died" after nearly every name.

Genesis 6.audience: Israel's neighbors in Mesopotamia told their own flood stories, such as the account of Utnapishtim in the Epic of Gilgamesh. Israelite hearers would recognize the subject while hearing it told with one God as the judge and rescuer.

culture.title: The cubit
culture.text: A cubit was the length from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, roughly 18 inches (45 centimeters). By that measure the ark was about 450 feet long, 75 feet wide, and 45 feet high.

culture.title: Pitch
culture.text: Bitumen, a natural tar, was used across Mesopotamia to waterproof boats and baskets. Moses' mother coated his basket with "slime and with pitch" (Exodus 2:3).

Genesis 7.audience: Israel's sacrificial law distinguished clean from unclean animals (Leviticus 11). Hearers would notice that the distinction already appears here, with seven of every clean beast taken into the ark (Genesis 7:2).

culture.title: The calendar of the flood
culture.text: The flood is dated by year, month, and day of Noah's life, the way ancient records dated events by a ruler's years. The narrative tracks the waters for about a year (Genesis 8:13–14).

Genesis 8.audience: Israelite readers knew Ararat as a land to the far north; it is later named as the place where the sons of Sennacherib fled (2 Kings 19:37). It corresponds to the region of Urartu, around modern eastern Turkey and Armenia.

culture.title: Birds sent from ships
culture.text: Ancient sailors released birds to find land; a bird that did not return had found somewhere to settle. The Mesopotamian flood story in the Epic of Gilgamesh also includes the release of a dove, a swallow, and a raven.

culture.title: A sweet savour
culture.text: "A sweet savour" is the same phrase Israel's law uses for burnt offerings accepted by the LORD (Leviticus 1:9).

Genesis 9.audience: Israel's food laws forbade eating blood (Leviticus 17:10–14). Hearers would recognize that rule's earliest form here, given to Noah for all humanity (Genesis 9:4).

culture.title: Covenant signs
culture.text: Ancient agreements were often marked by a visible sign or witness, such as a heap of stones (Genesis 31:44–48). The rainbow is the sign of God's covenant with every living creature, just as circumcision later becomes the sign of the covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17:11).

culture.title: Canaan
culture.text: Canaan, Ham's son, is the ancestor of the peoples living in the land Israel later entered (Genesis 10:15–19).

Genesis 10.audience: This list of nations names peoples Israel knew: Mizraim (Egypt), Cush, Canaan, Asshur (Assyria), the cities of Babel and Nineveh, and the Canaanite clans whose borders are traced from Sidon to Gaza (Genesis 10:19).

culture.title: Seventy nations
culture.text: The names in the table of nations total about seventy. The number recurs in Israel's story: seventy members of Jacob's family went down to Egypt (Genesis 46:27), and Moses appointed seventy elders (Numbers 11:16).

culture.title: Nimrod's cities
culture.text: Babel, Erech (Uruk), Accad, and Nineveh were real cities of Mesopotamia. Uruk was one of the world's earliest cities, and Nineveh later became the capital of Assyria.

Genesis 11.audience: For Israelite hearers, Babel was Babylon, the great city of Mesopotamia. The chapter also traces Abram's family from Shem to Ur of the Chaldees and Haran.

culture.title: Brick and bitumen
culture.text: Mesopotamia had little stone, so builders used baked brick set in bitumen, exactly as the verse says: "they had brick for stone, and slime had they for morter." In Canaan, by contrast, building in stone was normal.

culture.title: Ziggurats
culture.text: Mesopotamian cities built ziggurats—stepped temple towers of brick rising high above the plain. The great ziggurat of Babylon was known as Etemenanki.

Genesis 12.audience: Every place Abram passes through—Shechem, Bethel, Ai, and the Negev ("the south")—was land Israel later lived in. Hearers would know these places as their own towns.

culture.title: Building altars
culture.text: Abram builds altars as he moves through the land. In the ancient world, an altar marked a place of worship and laid a claim to the god's presence there; Israel's later law permitted altars of earth or uncut stone (Exodus 20:24–25).

culture.title: Famine and Egypt
culture.text: Canaan depended on rain, while Egypt was watered by the yearly flooding of the Nile. In drought, people from Canaan went down to Egypt for food, as Jacob's sons did later (Genesis 42:1–3).

Genesis 13.audience: The cities of the plain—Sodom and Gomorrah—were remembered in Israel as a byword for judgment (Deuteronomy 29:23). Hearers knew the region near the Dead Sea as barren, in contrast to how it looked before.

culture.title: Herders and grazing land
culture.text: Large flocks needed wide pastures and wells. When herds grew too big for the same land, herdsmen quarreled, and families separated to find grazing—a common pattern among pastoral peoples.

culture.title: Walking the land
culture.text: Walking through a land's length and breadth could signify taking possession of it. God later tells Joshua, "Every place that the sole of your foot shall tread upon, that have I given unto you" (Joshua 1:3).

Genesis 14.audience: Israelite hearers would recognize Salem as the old name associated with Jerusalem (Psalm 76:2) and Dan as the northern border town of their own day, which was called Laish before the tribe of Dan renamed it (Judges 18:29).

culture.title: Coalitions of city-kings
culture.text: Canaan was divided among many small city-states, each with its own king, and powerful eastern kings demanded tribute from them. Rebellion meant refusing tribute, which led to punitive campaigns.

culture.title: A tenth of the spoil
culture.text: Giving a tenth was a known practice in the ancient Near East. Abram gives Melchizedek a tenth of everything, and Israel later gave a tenth of its produce and herds to the LORD (Leviticus 27:30–32).

Genesis 15.audience: Israel heard this promise as the origin of their own story: their ancestors' time as strangers in Egypt, the four hundred years of affliction, and the return to Canaan (Genesis 15:13–16).

culture.title: Cutting a covenant
culture.text: In the ancient Near East, parties to a covenant sometimes walked between the halves of slaughtered animals, invoking the same fate on themselves if they broke it. Jeremiah describes the same rite (Jeremiah 34:18–19). Here only the smoking furnace and burning lamp pass between the pieces (Genesis 15:17).

culture.title: A household heir
culture.text: A childless man could name a trusted servant as heir. Abram's words about Eliezer of Damascus reflect that practice.

Genesis 16.audience: Israel's neighbors to the south and east included the Ishmaelite tribes, traders and desert dwellers (Genesis 37:25). This chapter tells of their ancestor's birth.

culture.title: A surrogate wife
culture.text: Ancient marriage contracts sometimes allowed a childless wife to give her servant to her husband so that a child could be counted as hers. Rachel and Leah later do the same with Bilhah and Zilpah (Genesis 30:3–9).

culture.title: The Angel of the LORD
culture.text: This is the first appearance in Scripture of "the angel of the LORD." Hagar names the place's well Beerlahairoi (Genesis 16:14).

Genesis 17.audience: Every Israelite male was circumcised on the eighth day (Leviticus 12:3). Hearers knew this chapter as the origin of that practice and of the names Abraham and Sarah.

culture.title: Circumcision in the ancient world
culture.text: Circumcision was practiced by several ancient peoples, including Egyptians, often at puberty or before marriage. In Abraham's family it was done on the eighth day after birth and served as the sign of the covenant.

culture.title: New names
culture.text: Abram means ‘exalted father’; Abraham is explained in the text as "a father of many nations." A new name marked a new status or role.

Genesis 18.audience: Hospitality to travelers was a deeply held duty in Israel, and its law repeatedly commands care for the stranger (Leviticus 19:33–34). Hearers would note how fully Abraham provides for his guests.

culture.title: Desert hospitality
culture.text: A host offered water for washing feet, rest in the shade, bread, and—for honored guests—meat, which was rarely eaten. Abraham calls it "a morsel of bread" and then serves a calf, cakes, butter, and milk.

culture.title: The tent door
culture.text: Sitting at the tent door in the heat of the day, the head of the household could see who approached. Women stayed inside the tent, which is why Sarah overhears from behind Abraham (Genesis 18:10).

Genesis 19.audience: Israel's eastern neighbors, Moab and Ammon, are traced here to Lot (Genesis 19:37–38). Israel's law later commanded them not to harass these nations because they were Lot's descendants (Deuteronomy 2:9, 19).

culture.title: The city gate
culture.text: The gate was the public center of an ancient town, where elders met, cases were judged, and business was done (Ruth 4:1–2). Lot sitting in the gate suggests he had standing in Sodom.

culture.title: Protecting a guest
culture.text: A host was bound to protect anyone who came "under the shadow of my roof." Lot's desperate offer shows how far that obligation was held to go. A similar scene occurs in Gibeah (Judges 19:22–24).

Genesis 20.audience: Gerar lay in the Negev near the coast, in the region later occupied by the Philistines. Hearers would know it as border country to the southwest.

culture.title: Kings taking wives
culture.text: Ancient kings added women to their households to build alliances and display power. A man's wife was protected from this, but an unmarried sister was not—which is why Abraham calls Sarah his sister.

culture.title: A thousand pieces of silver
culture.text: Before coins, silver was weighed out in shekels. A thousand pieces of silver was a large payment, given publicly to clear Sarah's honor.

Genesis 21.audience: Beersheba was the southern end of Israel's land in the familiar phrase "from Dan even to Beersheba" (Judges 20:1). This chapter explains the town's name.

culture.title: Weaning feast
culture.text: Children were often nursed for two or three years. Surviving infancy was a milestone, and families marked a child's weaning with a celebration.

culture.title: Wells and oaths
culture.text: In dry country, wells were valuable property and frequent causes of dispute. Abraham gives seven ewe lambs as a witness that he dug the well; Beersheba means ‘well of the oath’ or ‘well of seven.’

Genesis 22.audience: Israel's law forbade child sacrifice, which some neighboring peoples practiced (Leviticus 18:21; 2 Kings 3:27). Hearers would note that Isaac is spared and a ram offered instead. Moriah is later named as the site of Solomon's temple (2 Chronicles 3:1).

culture.title: Burnt offering
culture.text: A burnt offering was entirely consumed on the altar rather than shared in a meal. Abraham brings the wood, the fire (carried as coals), and a knife—the materials Israel's priests later used (Leviticus 1:7–9).

culture.title: Naming places
culture.text: Abraham names the place Jehovahjireh, ‘the LORD will provide.’ The text adds a saying still current when it was written: "In the mount of the LORD it shall be seen."

Genesis 23.audience: Hebron was an important town in Judah where David first reigned (2 Samuel 2:1–4). Israel knew the cave of Machpelah there as the burial place of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and their wives (Genesis 49:29–31).

culture.title: Buying land at the gate
culture.text: Property sales were done publicly before the town's elders at the gate, so that witnesses could confirm them. The courteous offers to give the land for free were a polite form of bargaining before naming a price.

culture.title: Silver by weight
culture.text: Abraham weighs out four hundred shekels of silver "current money with the merchant"—silver of the standard weight accepted in trade, since coins had not yet been invented.

Genesis 24.audience: Israel's law later discouraged marriage with Canaanites (Deuteronomy 7:3). Hearers would understand why Abraham sends to his own relatives in Mesopotamia for Isaac's wife.

culture.title: Oath under the thigh
culture.text: Placing a hand under the thigh was a solemn form of oath, probably connected with descendants and family. Jacob asks Joseph for the same oath (Genesis 47:29).

culture.title: Arranged marriage and gifts
culture.text: Marriages were arranged between families. The groom's side gave gifts—jewelry, clothing, and valuables—to the bride and her family. Rebekah's brother Laban takes a leading role in the negotiations.

culture.title: Watering camels
culture.text: A thirsty camel can drink many gallons of water. Offering to water ten camels meant drawing water from the well again and again—a sign of extraordinary generosity.

Genesis 25.audience: Israel's neighbors to the southeast, the Edomites, descended from Esau (Genesis 36:1). Hearers knew of the long rivalry between Israel and Edom, reflected in the struggle of the twins.

culture.title: The birthright
culture.text: The firstborn son normally received a double share of the inheritance and leadership of the family (Deuteronomy 21:17). Esau sells this right for a single meal.

culture.title: Lentil stew
culture.text: Lentils were a common, cheap food in the ancient Near East. The red color of the stew is the reason given for Esau's other name, Edom, meaning ‘red’ (Genesis 25:30).
